1 The story

One last session

Riya’s semester exam in Big Data is next week. Kabir has just received his full-time offer from TiffinGo, and the first thing he does is call Riya to help her revise. Arjun Sir joins them for one last session.

R> Sir, there’s so much. 5 Vs, CAP, Spark, Kafka, Parquet, DPDP… where do I even start? A> With the map, Riya. Every lesson answers one of four questions: what is big data, how do we store and spread it, which tools process it, and how do we keep it trustworthy and useful. If you can place each topic on that map, you can write any answer. K> In my interviews, they never asked definitions alone. Always “why” and “what if”. A> Exams reward the same thing in long answers: a definition, a diagram, an example and a trade-off. Today you get a one-page cheat sheet, the 2-mark and 5-mark answer patterns, a 50-mark practice paper you can regenerate on your PC, and a final test across the whole course. R> And if I score well on the final test? A> Then you’re ready, for the exam and for Kabir’s kind of interviews.
2 Definition

Big Data Fundamentals in one page

Formal definition (write this in exams)

Big Data Fundamentals covers the characteristics of data sets too large, fast or varied for a single traditional system (volume, velocity, variety, veracity, value); the storage formats and databases suited to them; the distributed-systems principles of scaling out, partitioning, replication and consistency; the ecosystem of processing and streaming tools (Hadoop, Spark, Kafka, lakehouse table formats, orchestration, cloud services); the practices of data quality, governance, security and privacy; and the roles and skills of data professionals, applied in an end-to-end pipeline.

In simple words

Big data is data too big, fast or messy for one computer. We spread it across many machines, store it in efficient formats, process it with tools like Spark and Kafka, keep it correct, safe and lawful, and turn it into useful answers.

LEVELS> Revision at three levels L1> Remember the core
  • Big data: 5 Vs; why one machine fails (disk speed, memory, single point of failure); scale out.
  • Data: structured, semi-structured, unstructured; CSV, JSON, Avro, Parquet, ORC; files, blocks, objects; NoSQL types.
  • Systems: partitioning, replication (factor 3), CAP, consistency levels.
  • Tools: HDFS, YARN, MapReduce, Hive, Spark, Kafka, lakehouse; Airflow; AWS/Azure/GCP equivalents.
L2> Explain and compare
  • Row vs columnar; lake vs warehouse vs lakehouse; batch vs streaming; ETL vs ELT; MapReduce vs Spark.
  • Scale up vs scale out; leader-follower vs leaderless replication; strong vs eventual consistency.
  • Mod-N hashing vs consistent hashing; provisioned vs serverless cloud.
  • Six data quality dimensions; governance components; DPDP rights and duties.
L3> Apply and design
  • Estimate load: totals → per second → peak; storage with replication and retention.
  • Design a pipeline: requirements, ingestion, bronze/silver/gold, orchestration, quality, idempotency, cost and governance.
  • Diagnose: skew, small files, wrong numbers (lineage), duplicates (idempotency), cost spikes (scans, idle clusters).
  • Case studies: UPI, IRCTC Tatkal, live cricket streaming, sale days.
/LEVELS EXAM> A full-marks long answer has five parts: definition (1–2 lines), diagram (labelled), explanation (points, not paragraphs), example (preferably Indian and with numbers) and advantages/limitations or a comparison table. Underline key terms.

Cheat sheet: comparisons examiners love

CompareFirstSecond
Scale up vs scale outBigger machine; simple; hard ceiling; single point of failureMore machines; near-linear growth; needs distribution and fault tolerance
Row vs columnarCSV, Avro: good for writing whole recordsParquet, ORC: good for reading few columns of many rows
Lake vs warehouseRaw files, any type, cheap, schema-on-readModelled tables, SQL, fast, schema-on-write
Batch vs streamingBounded data, scheduled, minutes to hoursUnbounded events, continuous, milliseconds to seconds
MapReduce vs SparkDisk between every step, Java-heavyIn-memory DAG execution, SQL/Python APIs, much faster for iterative work
CP vs APRefuse or delay to stay consistent (payments)Answer with possibly stale data (feeds, carts)
ETL vs ELTTransform before loadingLoad raw, transform inside the warehouse/lakehouse

4 Step by step

A revision plan that works

  1. Map before memorising

    Write the seven modules on one page and, under each, the lessons and three key words from memory. Fill gaps from the cheat sheet.

    A mental map makes every answer easier to place and connect.

  2. Practise recall, not rereading

    day1, day3, day7 = "learn", "recall", "recall again"
for d, task in [(1, day1), (3, day3), (7, day7)]:
    print(f"day {d}: {task}")
    day 1: learn day 3: recall day 7: recall again
    Testing yourself after a gap (day 1, day 3, day 7) builds memory far better than rereading notes.

  3. Use answer patterns

    2 marks: definition + one example or point. 5 marks: definition, diagram, 3–4 points, example. 10 marks: add comparison table, case study, advantages and limitations.

    Patterns stop you writing too much for small questions and too little for big ones.

  4. Take a timed paper

    Generate a paper with the program in “Run it on your PC”, write answers in 2 hours, then check against the lessons.

    Timing matters: about 22 minutes per 10 marks leaves 10 minutes to revise.

  5. Fix weak areas

    Note every question you struggled with, revisit that lesson’s Revision and FAQ sections, and redo its quiz.

    Targeted revision on weak lessons gives the biggest improvement per hour.

  6. Final test

    Take the 25-question final test on this page. Aim for 20 or more; review explanations for every mistake.

    It samples every module, so your score shows where you stand overall.
5 See it happen

A 5-mark answer: what Riya writes, and how it is marked

Step through the six frames. Left: Riya’s answer sheet. Right: the examiner’s marking scheme.

What Riya writes, and how it is marked 6 steps
What you see
  1. Riya reads a 5-mark question on the CAP theorem.
  2. She writes a precise definition first.
  3. She draws a small labelled diagram of a network partition.
  4. She explains C, A and P in short points.
  5. She adds examples: UPI balances (CP) and social-media likes (AP).
  6. She finishes with a limitation and the PACELC extension.
Behind the screen
  1. Marking schemes for 5-mark questions typically look for about five distinct elements.
  2. A precise definition earns the first mark.
  3. A diagram earns a mark in seconds and makes the answer easy to check.
  4. Explaining each property separately earns the explanation mark.
  5. Real examples prove understanding rather than memorising.
  6. A limitation or extension (no partition means both are possible; PACELC adds the latency vs consistency trade-off) earns the last mark. Schemes vary by university; this is a typical pattern.

Real-time scenario 2

An estimation question, solved for full marks

Numbers questions reward clear steps and stated assumptions more than exact answers. Watch one solved line by line, using UPI-scale figures.

Estimation 5 steps
Animated example
  1. Start by writing what you will compute and how: totals → per second → peak → storage.
  2. 24 billion ÷ (30 × 86,400 seconds) ≈ 9,300 transactions per second on average.
  3. Peaks are higher. State an assumption (4× the average) and design for about 37,000 TPS.
  4. Assume each transaction record is about 1 KB: 24 billion × 12 months × 1 KB ≈ 288 TB a year.
  5. With a replication factor of 3, about 864 TB, or roughly 0.9 PB, a year. Each assumption is written down, so the examiner can follow and award marks even if their numbers differ.
Real-time scenario 3 · advanced

One 10-mark case, every module

The best long answers pull ideas from across the course. Watch a railway booking case answered module by module, the structure that earns top marks.

Integrated case answer 5 steps
Animated example
  1. Begin with scale from published numbers: 37,410 tickets in one minute is about 624 per second at peak, with far more searches. This shows volume and velocity (Module 1).
  2. Choose storage: bookings in a strongly consistent transactional store, logs and history as Parquet in a lake, and a cache for seat availability pages (Module 2).
  3. Spread the load: partition by train and date, replicate across zones; seat allocation needs consistency (CP), while search results can be slightly stale (AP) (Module 3).
  4. Process: booking and search events flow into Kafka; Spark builds demand forecasts and detects bots; a waiting room protects the booking system at 10 am (Module 4).
  5. Trust: quality checks on booking data, passenger personal data protected under the DPDP Act, masked for analysts, with breach plans (Module 5). Add a diagram and a limitations paragraph for full marks.

Exam question bank

Answer each aloud or on paper before opening the model answer. Long answers should follow the five-part pattern: definition, diagram, explanation, example, limitations.

2-mark questions with model answers

Define big data.

Data sets whose volume, velocity or variety exceed the capacity of traditional single-machine systems to store and process them in acceptable time, requiring distributed storage and processing.

What is veracity?

The quality and trustworthiness of data: accuracy, completeness and consistency. Example: duplicate or fake transactions reduce veracity.

Differentiate structured and semi-structured data.

Structured data has a fixed schema of rows and columns (a bank table); semi-structured data has tags or keys but a flexible schema (JSON, XML).

What is a NameNode?

The HDFS master that stores the file system metadata (file names, block locations) and coordinates DataNodes, which store the actual blocks.

What is schema-on-read?

The schema is applied when data is read rather than when it is written, as in data lakes; allows storing raw data first.

What is a partition key?

The column whose value decides which partition or shard a row belongs to, for example customer_id or date.

What is eventual consistency?

If no new updates occur, all replicas eventually converge to the same value; reads may briefly return stale data.

What is a DAG in Spark or Airflow?

A directed acyclic graph of steps with dependencies and no cycles; Spark uses it for stages of computation, Airflow for task order.

What is a Kafka offset?

The sequential position of a message within a partition, used by consumers to track what they have read.

What is the lakehouse?

An architecture combining low-cost lake storage with warehouse features (ACID transactions, schemas, fast SQL) using table formats such as Delta Lake, Iceberg or Hudi.

What is egress in cloud billing?

Charges for data transferred out of a cloud region or out of the cloud, often a hidden cost.

Who is a data fiduciary under the DPDP Act?

The person or organisation that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data.

5-mark questions with answer outlines

Explain the 5 Vs of big data with examples.

Define each V in one line with an Indian example: volume (UPI billions a month), velocity (live cricket concurrency), variety (text, images, logs), veracity (fake reviews, duplicates), value (fraud detection, recommendations). Add a small diagram of the five Vs.

Why is one computer not enough for big data?

Disk read speed limits (hours to scan TBs), memory limits, CPU limits, single point of failure, cost of very large machines. Solution: split data and work across many machines (parallelism) with replication. Include a calculation, e.g. 10 TB at 200 MB/s ≈ 14 hours vs 100 machines ≈ 8 minutes.

Compare CSV, JSON, Avro, Parquet and ORC.

Table with: row/columnar, schema, compression, splittable, best use. CSV/JSON human-readable but large; Avro row-based with schema, good for streaming and Kafka; Parquet/ORC columnar, compressed, best for analytics.

Explain replication strategies.

Leader-follower (writes to leader, followers copy; sync vs async), multi-leader, leaderless with quorums (R + W > N). Benefits: availability, durability, read scaling; issues: lag, conflicts, failover. Diagram.

Explain Spark architecture.

Driver, cluster manager, executors; jobs, stages, tasks; lazy evaluation and DAG; narrow vs wide transformations and shuffles; in-memory processing. Diagram with driver and executors.

Explain Kafka architecture.

Producers, brokers, topics, partitions, offsets, replication, consumer groups; ordering per partition; retention; use cases like UPI events or order tracking. Diagram.

Explain cloud service models for big data with AWS/Azure/GCP examples.

IaaS, managed PaaS, serverless, SaaS; examples: S3/ADLS/GCS, EMR/Databricks/Dataproc, Redshift/Synapse/BigQuery; benefits and concerns (cost, lock-in, residency).

Explain the DPDP Act, 2023 from a data engineer’s point of view.

Fiduciary and principal; consent and notice; purpose limitation; rights (access, correction, erasure); security safeguards; breach notification within 72 hours to the Board; penalties up to ₹250 crore; engineering impacts: PII tagging, masking, deletion workflows, audit logs.

10-mark questions to practise

  • Design a data pipeline for a food-delivery company’s daily revenue dashboard (use your capstone).
  • Explain how a platform like IRCTC handles the Tatkal spike, with calculations (Lesson 4.7).
  • Describe the Hadoop ecosystem and compare it with Spark and the modern lakehouse.
  • Explain partitioning, replication and consistency in distributed databases with diagrams.
  • Explain data quality, governance and security for a big data platform, including the DPDP Act.
